extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary critics, advanced readers of fiction (particularly those studying Proust)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic method and terminology for describing narrative discourse in fiction (distinguishing story, narrative, and the act of narrating; cataloguing temporal, focal, and voice-related operations). Emphasizes systematic classification illustrated with Proust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold distinction: story, narrative, narrating
rubrics_metrics.description: Use distinct terms for three senses of 'narrative': (1) story = the signified / the succession of events (diegesis); (2) narrative = the signifier, the discourse or text that tells those events; (3) narrating = the act of producing the narrative (the enunciating act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should keep these levels distinct because only the narrative (the discourse) is directly available to textual analysis; the events (story) and the narrating act are known only indirectly through traces in the narrative (e.g., tense, person). Confusing these senses produces conceptual ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish focalization (mood) from voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate the question 'who is the character whose point of view orients the narrative perspective?' (focalization/mood) from the question 'who is the narrator?' (voice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same point of view (focalization) can be narrated either by a first‑person narrator or by a third‑person narrator; conversely, first‑person narration can vary in focalization depending on whether events are seen from the narrator's present consciousness or his past consciousness. Treating these as one confuses central analytic categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vs. external focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal focalization: narrative is focused through a character's consciousness (we are given their perceptions/ thoughts). External focalization: narrative is focused on a character but not through his consciousness (we are told what characters do, not what they think or see).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate external focalization with another form of internal focalization; critics (e.g., Mieke Bal) argue that treating these very different cases as variants weakens the concept. Use emendations where necessary to keep precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order (anachronies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the temporal order of events in the story with the order in which they are narrated; mismatches yield devices like flashback, foreshadowing, in medias res.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and name permutations of story-order vs narrative-order. Order is a primary axis for describing how narrative rearranges events and produces effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration / pace
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how much narrative space is devoted to a given portion of story time (e.g., extended scene, summary, ellipsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast scene (mimetic, detailed treatment of a brief event) with summary (condensed account spanning longer story time). Duration/pace determines narrative emphasis and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency (the iterative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether events that happened once are narrated repeatedly, or events that happened frequently are narrated once; classify modes of repetition (e.g., iterative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequency has been under-discussed but is crucial: repetition is central to certain modern/avant‑garde techniques. Identify iterative modes and their narrative functions (emphatic, thematic, structuring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-iterative
rubrics_metrics.description: A figure in which the narrative represents something as having happened repeatedly when, within the story, particular details imply singularity (presenting singular events as if they were habitual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize pseudo-iterative constructions (e.g., long accounts embedded in a supposedly repeated weekly routine) and analyze their strange effects; they can render the singular as seemingly collective or habitual and produce anomalies in temporal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mood: mimesis vs diegesis and polymodality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mood concerns the degree to which events are shown (mimesis) or told (diegesis); some narratives exhibit polymodality—mixing or transgressing these modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect moments where 'showing' and 'telling' blur (e.g., when observational scenes include access to characters' thoughts). Such mixing can be problematic for rigid models and must be marked as 'polymodality' or anomaly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice: narrative levels and transgressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Map who is speaking (narrator identity, narrative levels) and note movements between levels; in complex texts (e.g., Proust) shifts between narrative levels can be confused, transgressive, and constitutive of style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify level shifts (e.g., embedded narratives, narrator commenting on narration) and evaluate whether they follow a stable hierarchy or produce deliberate transgressions that affect interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative enunciating (the act of narrating) as analytic object
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the narrating act itself (who utters the narrative, under what fictional/practical conditions) as essential—distinct from the author's real act of writing—and analyze its traces within the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because narrating is the source of the discourse, pay attention to indices in the text (person, tense, explicit signals) that reveal the narrating situation. Do not substitute biographical facts about the author for the narrating situation of the fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anomalies and exceptions diagnostically
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider bizarre or exceptional narrative techniques (those that violate the 'model of the real world') as diagnostically important: anomalies can reveal and even determine normative categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a work repeatedly violates assumed narrative models (e.g., impossible combinations of knowledge/ignorance), analyze these violations to refine or extend analytic categories rather than dismiss them as noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic taxonomy of narrative figures and devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an organized terminology (figures, categories, operations) to identify and describe the constituents and techniques of narrative rather than relying on ad hoc, piecemeal labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A systematic poetics should name devices (e.g., anachronies, iterative, focalization types) and show relations among them; test the taxonomy rigorously against complex texts and be open to emendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological balance: theory and criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ theory to clarify and generalize descriptive observations, while using careful critical (textual) analysis to ground and constrain theoretical claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating a text merely as an example or reducing analysis to abstract 'laws' divorced from particulars; conversely, use particular texts to reveal universal elements. The method oscillates between particular close reading and general classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminological precision (avoid common‑usage slippage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because ordinary usage of terms like 'narrative' is ambiguous, maintain terminological precision to prevent confusions in analysis (e.g., explicitly define how 'narrative' is being used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State definitions at the outset and adhere to them (e.g., 'story' for content, 'narrative' for discourse, 'narrating' for the act). This precision is necessary for cumulative theoretical work.
